Yet Taha Hussein himself devotes fifty-five pages of his book to discussing the political, religious, and other reasons why Muslims fabricated large amounts of poetry and attributed it to pre-Islamic poets.
If this fabrication was to serve its intended purposes, then those producing it naturally had to imitate the pre-Islamic poets in the poetry or prose they attributed to them.
The fabricated poems therefore had to resemble genuine pre-Islamic poetry as closely as possible in language, style, subject matter, content, description, imagery, and other historical features.
That required the fabricators to possess a broad knowledge of all these features.

It also required considerable literary skill. They had to absorb those features well enough to produce poetry with a convincingly pre-Islamic form and identity, while hiding as far as possible every sign that the poem had actually been written during the Islamic period.
Most or all of these conditions existed among the Muslim transmitters, hadith scholars, Qurʾānic commentators, and theologians who fabricated such poetry.
Taha Hussein himself gives evidence of this.
He reports what the Kufan transmitter al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī said about Ḥammād al-Rāwiya:
When al-Mufaḍḍal was asked why—whether Ḥammād made grammatical mistakes or other errors—he replied:

“If only that were the problem. Scholars can correct a man who makes mistakes. But Ḥammād knows the dialects of the Arabs, the styles of the poets, and their meanings. He keeps composing poetry in the style of one poet and inserting it into that man’s work. It is then transmitted from him far and wide, until the poetry of the ancient poets becomes mixed together and the genuine can be distinguished from the false only by a truly knowledgeable critic. And where is such a critic to be found?”

The qualities described here—both Ḥammād’s method of fabrication and his deep knowledge of Arab dialects—were probably shared by many of those who fabricated poetry and attributed it to the pre-Islamic period during the age when oral traditions were being collected and books were being written.
If that is so, then poetry fabricated under these conditions must preserve many of the main features, qualities, and historical meanings of genuine pre-Islamic poetry.
Otherwise the fabrication would fail both as a literary exercise and in whatever religious, political, linguistic, or historical purpose it was meant to serve.

The claim about Ḥammād al-Rāwiya would otherwise make no sense: that he could continually compose poetry in the style of an earlier poet, insert it into that poet’s work, and spread it so widely that genuine and fabricated ancient poetry became almost impossible to distinguish except by an expert critic.
For this reason, a scientific researcher cannot follow Taha Hussein in his categorical judgments.

We cannot accept the claim that “the overwhelming majority of what we call pre-Islamic literature has nothing to do with the pre-Islamic period,” or that it is “Islamic, reflecting the life, tendencies, and passions of Muslims far more than the life of the pre-Islamic Arabs.”

Nor can we accept that the small amount of genuine pre-Islamic literature that remains “represents nothing and proves nothing,” or that it should not be used to reconstruct an accurate literary picture of the pre-Islamic period.
The same applies to his statement that the poems attributed “to Imruʾ al-Qays, al-Aʿshā, or other pre-Islamic poets (...) prove nothing and tell us nothing.”
A scientific historical method requires a different approach.

We must treat pre-Islamic poetry—both the genuine poetry and the later fabrications—as living historical material with a real and objective connection to Arab social reality during two closely overlapping periods: the pre-Islamic period immediately before Islam and the early Islamic period immediately after it.
For our purposes here, this means looking closely at all the historical meanings found throughout the surviving body of poetry known to us as pre-Islamic poetry.
Those meanings are as varied as the social reality to which the poetry points.
The ancient Arabs themselves instinctively recognized that pre-Islamic poetry carried this kind of historical meaning when they said that poetry was the record of the Arabs.
They seem to have meant that poetry preserved Arab history itself, which is also suggested by the word dīwān, or record.
When they spoke of “poetry” in this expression, they meant pre-Islamic poetry.

Among all Arabic poetry, this was the one body of poetry that did not need to be identified by the historical period in which it was produced. For them, it alone deserved to be called the record of the Arabs.

Likewise, the word “Arabs” in this expression naturally meant the Arabs of the pre-Islamic period, just as it did in traditional expressions such as “the battle-days of the Arabs,” “the markets of the Arabs,” and “the speech of the Arabs.”

By the historical meaning of pre-Islamic poetry, we mean everything in its content that expresses, through the poetic language of its time, the historical features that distinguish pre-Islamic Arab society from Arab society in the centuries after Islam.
These features concern both social reality and social consciousness.
The historical meanings that concern us here therefore have two main dimensions: a social dimension and a dimension of knowledge and thought.
The level reached by pre-Islamic poetry has to be judged according to its own historical period.
For that reason, it represents an earlier stage of development than Arabic poetry in the more advanced Arab-Islamic centuries—for example, the fourth Islamic century.
At this earlier stage, pre-Islamic poetry, like poetic art generally at a similar level of development, reflects social reality in direct, relatively flat, and highly detailed language.
It belongs to a stage at which poetry has not yet moved from being one particular way of recounting reality to becoming the artistic creation of a new reality of its own.
This is why the social world of the pre-Islamic period appears in such detail in the poetry of that period—or in poetry attributed to it.
A modern researcher can move quite easily from the poetic scene described in a verse to the social event or social reality behind it.
The distance between the two is short, simple, and direct.
This historical feature of pre-Islamic poetry may be the real basis for the old Arab saying that “poetry is the record of the Arabs.”
Another poetic feature goes with it.
Tribal social relations dominate the inner workings of pre-Islamic poetry almost completely.
The poet’s individual “self” appears only as one expression of this larger tribal relationship.
This is why the line between the poet speaking for himself and the tribe speaking through the poet becomes difficult to see.
The boundaries disappear, for example, between love poetry and war poetry:
I remembered you while spears drank deep of me, and Indian blades were dripping with my blood.
I longed to kiss the swords, because their flash was like the gleam of your smiling teeth.
The same happens between love poetry and poetry of pride, battle, praise, elegy, or any of the other traditional categories used to classify pre-Islamic verse.
Consider, for example, al-Munakhkhal ibn ʿĀmir al-Yashkurī and his poem beginning:
If you mean to reproach me, then go— go toward Iraq and do not turn back.
It is difficult to accept the traditional division of pre-Islamic poetry into separate categories.
It may make more sense to give the whole body of this poetry a single title:
the poetry of the Arab tribe before Islam.
But did the poetry of the ṣaʿālīk—the outlaw poets—possess some special feature that takes it outside this description?
The poetry of the outlaws contains a striking tension that may be one of the most important historical meanings found anywhere in pre-Islamic poetry.
On one side, it contains all the basic features of “the poetry of the Arab tribe before Islam.”
On the other, it contains all the elements of a rejection of that very world.
Yet these two sides do not reach the point of complete opposition or contradiction.
The outlaw poets did not write outside the linguistic and artistic forms of pre-Islamic tribal poetry.
Nor did they exist outside the economic and social relations of their age.
They wrote from a particular position within those relations—a position that expressed, in behavior, the beginning of their historical breakdown.
Their poetry therefore became an early and spontaneous form of awareness of this historical process.
It reflected the instability and loosening that had begun to affect the material foundations of tribal relations in Arabian society.
Within the tribe, social differences were developing between those who held positions of leadership and those who were subordinate.
These differences also produced growing material inequality, together with the oppression and suffering of one group at the hands of another.
This was the beginning of the breakdown we are describing.
It was also the first social source of the phenomenon of the ṣaʿālīk, the outlaws of pre-Islamic Arabia.
This social background produced the distinctive tension found in their poetry.
What makes their poetry unusual within the pre-Islamic tradition is its element of rejection: the rejection of tribal social relations at the point when those relations had reached maturity.

That rejection also involved resisting the tribe’s complete control over the poet’s individual self—the power of the tribal collective over the individual personality of the poet, a power that could almost completely surround and absorb that individuality.
ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward, one of these outlaw poets, put the issue with remarkable directness.
He compared two kinds of outlaw existing within the same social relations.
He expressed contempt for the first because this man submitted to the crushing conditions around him and accepted them.
He praised the second because he stood proud, rejected those conditions, and felt within himself the strength to overcome the obstacles holding back his ambitions.
1 — Of the first type, ʿUrwa says:
May God curse the outlaw who, when night falls, goes wandering among the paths, haunting every slaughtering place;
who counts himself rich whenever, for a night, he gains the hospitality of some well-off friend;
who rarely seeks wealth except for himself, until he stands like some weak, leaning shelter;
who sleeps early, then sits there in the morning, brushing the pebbles from his dust-covered side;
who helps the women of the camp whenever they ask, and ends the day exhausted like a worn-out camel.
2 — Of the second type, he says:
By God, what an outlaw—his face shines like the blaze of a newly kindled flame. (a)
He looks down upon his enemies as they drive him from their ground like a marked gaming arrow. (b)
And even when they are far away, they never feel safe from his return; they watch for him as a family watches for someone long absent. (c)
Such a man, if he meets death, meets it with honor; and if one day he becomes rich, he deserves it all the more. (d)
Yet this distinctive feature of the pre-Islamic outlaw poets does not take their poetry outside the basic feature shared by pre-Islamic poetry as a whole.
That feature is the dominance of historical meaning—especially social meaning—over all the other elements that make up the poetry.
Even its artistic qualities become a burden on the poetry itself, and on later Arabic poetry as well, if we strip them of this historical meaning.

For this reason, scientific research cannot form a complete picture of the pre-Islamic period without also reading that period through pre-Islamic poetry itself, carefully and comprehensively, taking into account the full body of surviving texts.
By the “knowledge dimension,” we mean the historical evidence in pre-Islamic poetry that can tell us something about how people at the time understood the universe and the world around them.
